div.head: TliE QUEEN'S SPEECH.
div.p: TliE QUEEN'S SPEECH.

PROBABILITIES OF AN EARLY LLSSOLUTIOR, The Queen's Speech, which we published on Thursday, is one of but scant promise. It is interesting as touch on ac. count of the many important questions that it leaves un- touched as of those to which some slight reference is mads. A few days ago there were 'holm who itnagined that it was the intention of the Government to go in for a lot of legisla- tive work during this the seventh Session of the present Parliament, and it was hinted that the speech would be in- dicative of the great things that the Ministry proposed to do before • dis.soluti,,n deprived them of their commanding majority. Well, oth the exception of the measures relating to Ireland, and which is a case of the most urgent news- Oily, very little is promised, and it is quite! certain that still less will he accomplished. On former occasions it has been the police of Lord Beaconsfield to hottna parole of Rills to he submitted to Parliament, which possibly it was never intended to pass, and which arta matter of fact rover wore passed. Baton this occasion, for reasons best known to himself different tactics ere adopted.

As usual when the Tories are in office, foreign affairs occupy by far the larger portion of the speech, ant as a matter of coulee out this occasion, the" Peace with honour " treaty ie made In occupy a foremeet place. In referring to the Berlin treaty, however, it will be noticed that the Government have found it impossible to congratulate them- selves on the work they haveaccomplished. On the contrary there is, he fact, an admission of failure. 0 Much," we are told, remake to be done to reptir the dieorder of the Turkiuh Empire, hut there in dui dellnite proposal how that "touch " is to be done. The reso,ne of affairs in Afghanistan leads up to an equally unsatisfactory result. There is no reference to lienerel Itoberts's barber°nt butcheries, and the Government don't toll us what position England is to occupy in the future with regard to Afghanistan, simply because they don't know. The attack on Afghaniman was an egregious and cruel blunder that has led rut into a mess, that nobody at present seems to see the..! out of. And eo all that is to he gathered from the Ministerial speech i,, that having reduced the country to a state of amechy, we must go on with our wrong-doing to the bitter end. A withdrawal of the hoots at present is asserted to be so irnpoesibility. Of course, there are great congratulations respecting the cruel Zulu war and the " capture and deposition" of poor . Celewavo. Credit in taloa for having relieved the South o frican colonies front a danger which has seriously impeded their advancement and consolidation." r lie Trans- vaal, we are also reminded, has born freed front the doper ila- tions of a powerful obictt hut the ilitlicolty with the Boers is not even referred to. All the ugly features in connection with °or invasions and annesatiode in South Afrina are, of course, kept In the background, and the accomplishment of the confederation scheme and the extension of s eyetent of ,clf.government is dwelt upon inn hopeful way, and eta cloak that will midi. to cover the multitude of sins that have been eumtnitted in tho English name in that part of the world.

With the exception of the p iragraph on Ireland, the review of events at home is scarce worthy of notice, and it is nuore than probable float thorn is no serious intention of dealing effectively with the few imam.mo that or inentioned. A bill for th, consoliabi. Con of the criminal law, a Bankruptcy Amendment Bill, a bill amen ling the Lunacy Act, and a bill, as we understand it, for granting greater fraxdorn of site to life mane. of landed properly, include the Government programme of home legislation for this, the last, semioro of a Parliament that has not been distinguidied for anything so much an the unwillingness or incapacity that It has betrayed from the commencetnent to carry tneasures of domestic improvement. The reference to the distrese in Ireland 14 somewhat myste- does ; and, with the knowledge that the suffering in some of the distressed districts is most acute, and that pamle ore actually already perishing of cold anal hunger, the Irbil, members most Wee listened with astonishment to the announoement that the authoritim charged with the duties of administering relief have been &lel upon "to make atnple preparation for the distribution of fool asd fuel, shodd sm•lt o step become nro,sary.'" If it has not b.come necessary weeks ago the accountr we have had from all unartem of the progress of the thane...LW utterly untruthful. The propmal to meet the relief ex- penditore out of the Irish Church surplus will doubtless re- ceive the sanctiott of Parliament. The pomoeal info pass a bill indemnifying the Government for advances of money made or to be made for the purpose of giving employment lin Ireland. 'These exceptional advance, are to be made on I the security of the properly administerad by the Church Temporalities Commissioners. But what about the many important measure. of which the speech inakes no mention, that have been poetponed session after session, 111114 for one or other of which people ate clamouring at every political gathering that take, place t Ireland is referred to, but there is no reference to the anti rent agitation, and no proposal to attempt legislation in the direction of giving relief to the tillers and occupiers of the tn the distressed farmers in either England or Ireland. There is no mention of. reform of local gkvernnient in the I I counties, of a corrupt practices at elections bill, of of. bill for; I assimilating the county and borough franchise, of. Burial. I I Bill, and of other bills of minor importance, many of which are never-tin les. ur,ntly r, qu ired. The Minieterial Speech on this occasion does not hold out any promise of a really useful session. There is no evidence of an intention on the part of the ministry to endeavour to redeem their character. by accomplishing & large amount of armful legislative work. floor. not in the mere, but may I not the true explanation of this omitous ailmce on such important nteasurs m those we have referred to be, that it ill i not the intention of the Premier to pmtpene the dis- solution to the end of the Session ? The appeal to the country may be made much sooner than ' many people hove of late been lot to expect

DOME RULERS AND CONSERVATIVES. The political contest at Liverpool he. had the effect of showing lion. Rulers who are the true and reliable friends ,of the Irish people. Lord Ramsay, the Lib.val candidate, when asked by the Home Rulers to pledge himself to vote for an inquiry into the necensity for • restoration of the Mali Parliament, deelinod. At another interview with the leaders of the Home Rule moviment it was explainel by his lord. ohip that he was opposed to a restoration of the Irish Par- , liament as it existed prior to its abolition, but that he dirt not object to vote for an inquiry into the alleged necissity of having a Parliament for Ireland lliis explanation I smoothed the way too reconciliation between the conch i lato and the Home Rule ito or, o reconciliati on that proved bitterness to the ministerbd organs and to the wile-pullers of Toryism. They aceneed Lord Hammy of coquetting with Home Rulers, and of being reely anti willing to disintegrate the empire if he could only win the Irish safe. Mn, A. M Sullivan, M.P., by the persoual attaek.s uporijaird Ramsay, has been goaded to "let the cat out of the bag," and the rx- posure to which he has subjected the wily trick. of the Conseriatives is one that is not likely to be soon formitten or hushed up. Speaking at Liverpool the other day, be ardonished his auditory by charging Lord Beaconsfield and his followers with being the authors of the Home Rule agitation, which the Tory press and orators h..ve bees no ready to publicly condemn as founded on tretson and mdition. Ile not only accumd the Tonic. of calmly and craftily originating the Home ilule movement, but ot mpporting it in its early stages by their purses. "It was," he said, "umin an invitation from the Conservative camp that the Iridi Nationalists commenced the movement ;- that able and bid amtial 0000ie, le.uleci, and representatives of the Conservative party SO premed upon the Irish poli- ticians the duty of participit ng in such a movement that their abstention would have been set down to sectarian mis- trust, animosity, or bigotry," that the Conservative, found the looney w Lich enabled some of the earlierit and most oevere contests for Home Rule to he fought, and, further supplied the funds for "the one open aad avowed Fenian candidature in Ireland ;" and that the agenm who were most successful in the establishment of the movement weie singled out for marks of favour by the leaders and cbiefs of the Conservative party. Such a revelation of political ras- cality might well astonod those to whom Mr. Sullivan I addreesed himself. This revelation he did not limit to his Imaiers, hut forwarded it for eati.n to a Jingo contemporary in Loudon, which ha: exercimil itself in eindunning Lord Ranmay fur after satisfactory explanations of a misapprehension of a phrase, put himself upon term, of friendsliip with members of the Hoine Rule party in Liverpool. Mr. Soi- llivan's exposure, which will be found in another column of I tkis day's Examiner, proves that the Tories, by craft and rsubtitle., nought to win the Irish vote. and to •ealien the ranks of the Liberals. Failing. however. in their iniquitona plot, they assumed an air of innocence cad patriotism mad . betook thmuselvis to denouncing the actirn of thou very Home Rale.. they had in secret placed= the war-tratb. TIIE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 7, IRO.
LINCAS I I IRE AND THE LIBERAL REACTION.

The wave of Liberal opinion that re .weeping over the country increases in volume, and there are many Cigna and gyorptonm of coming dioakers for Tory candidates at the next general eleotion. At Chaster, on Monday night, there wee a Conservative gathering, where Mr. !Luke, could woree get • hearing, and even the eloquence of Her 31 ajesty's General, Sir liardinge Gilitrd, did not suffice to quell the storm of opposition that woo raieed by . attempt to page a vote of confidence in the Govern- ment. Everywhere people are beginning to are the importance of the Vvcc that has to be tried at the next general election. Eye-Menu are being thrust aside, and the great question to simply eve of approval or dimpproval of Lord Beaconefield'e "Imperial" mode of governing the country, and of his pugeacroue foreign policy. What the Liberate are now fighting against in a foreigu policy of aggreesion and cruelty towards weak and serui.civilined etatm, and a general policy of, as Mr. Gladstone expremee it, " and reckless innovations." Even at places whore Coumrvative M.P.'a would a yeae or two ago Lam been listened to with patieooo and neon with approval, they now find that they have to encounter oppooition and hostile demonetratiotee In the coon' tier opinion doe, not change so rapidly as in tho large centres of population, and the last hope of the supportera of the Government is that the reaction will out prove strong ettrugh to effect county vote.. Yet even here there are signs of disaff.tion and revolt. The Tory squires thus aro diarturbed, and in varioue plee••s the county member. have been exhibit- ing gigue of un.ual activity. We hoar of them in their diff,rent diotrirke attending Coneervativa "tea fights," where addreases are delivered in detente of the Goveroment, tufortuuately for them it cannot I be uid that there ix, much of thin Conservative loratory that ix rot all calculated to win the support of waverers, or to nook° people admire tho spirit that animatee the rank and file of the Tory ' party at the present time. On the cons tury it he not too much to say that many of the j epeeches recently delivered by county representativ. have Keel the public mind the very uppwite effect from tbat which no doubt ig intended. We cannot • but think that if Lord Beacomelield could only find I time to read the addresses to their constiluenta of some of his most devoted followers, ho would despair of the party he hen been at such pains to educate. Amongst recent apologiste or advocas of modem Toryism are Messrs. Egertou and Hardee/ale, tho member. for South-East Lancashire. On Saturday evening they attended • meeting at Stretford, to inaugurate • " Canoe:votive A...lather for the district." The proceedierre were of the tamest deetriptiem, aud I the reception accorded must have had o rather • disquieting effect upon both gentlemen. If at au uolusively Conservative gathering to inaugurate j a load Conaervative Association, the members !for South•Emt Lancashire find that the I audience they addrem is not iu sympathy with their view., what kind of. reception arc they to expect when they come to appeol to the constituency ! at large? The "Laughter," and "oh, ohs," and I "granite" that were every now and regain drawn , foeeh by the assertiets of the speakers Imolts sa though the Stretford Conservative. are no great admirer. of , the Tory policy as expoanded by Means. Anginas's an Rusoous RAILWAY SNATION.—About twenty minutes past eight o'clock on Saturday evening • sad accident happened to Joseph Harrison, the captain of a boat, at Runcorn Railway Station. Hanison and his wife booked to Liverpool, and he appears to have been rather late in getting tickets, fur on leaving the booking °lN...they found the traM in the (Nati.. Harrison's wife attempted to cross behind the Liverpool train, which wan etanding ou the down line, and, owing to being very dull of hearing, she did not hear the approach of a luggage train from the oppo- site direction. Harrison, seeing his wife's danger, courage- ously rushed 10 save her, and was successful in so doing, but was unfortunately caught by the goods engine, aud knocked down In the" four-foot," four or trot the waggons passing over him, end cutting off his debt foot. The poor fellow was retnoved to the tome, of Ids sister, in Suffolk- street, and attended by Pr. McDougrll. We are glad to he able to state that HarrisT is progressing favourably.

IMPROVEMENTS ,ar WIDNES PARISH Curtacti.— Our readers will be pleased to hear that it has been decided, under the advice of the new Vicar, to effect several very necessary improvenients in the Widnes Parish Chmeh. The sacred edifice is in a most unfortunate location, being iinine- diately opposite the chemical works of Messrs. Hutchinson, the vapouis from which hare in past times found an easy entrance by means of the front loon, which had to be left open during Invine service. It has ben very wisely decided by the Vicar (the Bev. J. Wright Williams)and the church wardens to remedy this evil by closing up the door at the east side of the porch, and opening another in its place at the west end. Many complaints have been made of the want of Snot seats, and to remedy tnis defect tho organ has been re- to the pine where the east porch originally wag, using the space thus obtained for uxts of this description. The building is also being decorated by Messrs. Hesketh and Sons, of Bullet-market-street Wan ington, and will, we doubt not, when the work is completed, present an altogether different appemance, and one more worthy of 0 building devoted to Divine wtothip. two Wvottes Mrmomsv MLNISTER trio BMOMING IN RAILWAY CARRIAPES.—We understand that on Saturday night an outrage was committed upon the Rev. Jame. Hotchintion (Wesleyan Methodist), of lialtidah- terrace, Widnes. The rev. gentleman, on being applied to for some details 01 11,0 affair by our ',presentative, declined to give Any. We, however, may state that we are informed that on Saturday afternoon Mr. Hutchinson paid a visit to Manchester, and on his return begot into a third-class car- riage where several fellows of the tooter s nt" were smoking, and they refused to desist upon his asking them to It to. The result was that he give expression to his overworked feelings ill good homely Saxon; and on the train arriving at Bank Quay Station, Warringtvn, une of the IsetlM of the fragrant seed was remov,tl from the carriage by the guard, at the request of Mr. Hutchinson. However, as Mr. Hutchin- son was walking home, and had got opposite the branch of Parr's Bank, which is net very many yards from the London and North-Western Station, he was struck A violent blow on the lack of the head, which tendered him senseless. On coming to himself he gave information to a policeman, but by that time the assailant had made good usc of his heels, and was nowhere to be seen. Of course ills not accurately known that the man who committed the assault was one of Shore with whom Mr. Hutchinson had had the high words in the railway carriage, but it is supposed so. We believe that the matter has bent in the hands of the police—who have not, how!ver, given this informatlon—for.soine days.

Two STEEL ARROW S•reastentr COMPAMT, LIMITED. —We publish in another column a prospectnt of the Steel Arrow Steamship Company, Lhoited, which is being floated at a most opportune thne. The management of the venture is in the hands of a thoroughly practical man, Mr. Sprott, one of the joint managers, and well known in Whitehaven as a successful shipbuilder. It appears that the greater part of the shares of the company have already been subscribed, so that it is only the remaintler of the 320 sbires of £lOO each which are now offered. The Steel Arrow, the first of the 1 fleet to be built, is to he, steel-screw steamship, carrying 1,000 tons, and fitted as may be taken for granted, with every modeso appliance to render it unrivalled in the close of trade for which it is intended, viz., the mowing and profit- able one of conveying cattle and live stock. The vessel is now being constructed on the Clyde, and the benefit which the managers have secured in having let tie contracts before the revival in the iron and steel trade may be understood from the statement that since they were placed steel has rodeo price £7 per ton, which will give a great advantage to this company over any subsequent efforts to supply the demand for shipping which is now becoming apparent. The superiority of limited liability to the old system of dividing a ship 1010 01 notion ed shares is apparent, afford- ing much greater protection to the owmrs. The other 1 steamers to be built will be formed into companies on the same principle. Messrs. Jack and Co-, of Liverpool, are , constructing the mschineryomd tilt solicitors are Menem. 1 Banks and Kendall, Church-etrcet, Liverpool. th'e under. stand that the promotera of this really promising company are identified with similar undertakings, and posseee a large amount of influence in commercial circles. 1

1117.(7011N ORCIIINTRAL SOCIETV.—The secsnd annual concert of this society took place on Wednesday evening,in the Public Hall. The programme provided was a very varied one, comprising as it did selections front the works of I Rossini, Berger, Hadyn, Verdi, Gong'', and Strauss, and it I ought to have drawn together a for larger audience. It the members of the society had been advertised to appear with , their faces blacked. we have no doubt the Runcorn public would have gone in larger numbers; for it scorns to be the ca,e that only nigge.' companies and comic sismers are able to draw anything like an audience in the good old town. ' Those who stayed away on Wednesday night miss“l as decided tree. The members of the society have v,stly improved on their loot appearance; they played well toge- Inter and in Dine, and only ence or twice did we notice any unsteadiness in their time. Mr. Randall (of M. de Jorge handl took the placeof Mr.Dearden, and gave "The village blacksmith," and "The Death of Nelson," in fine style r,n the !rondo., which proved a most effective instrument in his hands. Mr. Fred Toss icon artist of great ability; he went through his arduous duties of accompanist and solo pianist to the I entire satisfaction of all. His playing with the bind was most judicious, and his solos characterised by great execu- tive pOwtt and fine feeling. The "Dial for piano (Mt. Pasch violin (Mr. C. Powell, and violoncello (51r.Simkin),1 by Haydn, in ti No. I, was rather scrambled through, Mr. Powell toes plenty of execution, and on this occasion he al-1 lowed himself to be carried 'away by it. Mr. Ravenscroft , was a very efficient conductor. The society are to be con- crateeed on their marked improvement. We are sorry to learn that they are likely to In•e Ed by their venture. The love of good music ia evidently at a very low ebb in Run- corn, for the only other local society of amateurs we have were losers atoned to the sante Amount, when they gave the ." VEMBER asked how it was that the report and balance- : sheet had not the number of members in the Society placed upon it, in the SHIlt manner as similar documents published by like organisations. tinder the present circumstances they did not know what their strength really ITTA and they were not able to say whether the Society was' progressing or retrograding. He proposed that the numbers should be placed upon the next report. (AppLmme.) The CHAIRMAN said he hod not the slightest objection to such ?.course being powmwl.

"-. A MEMBER exprene,,d hit wi 11' mgn,ss to second the pro- posal. (Applause.) Mr. Roma did not !Jelin,: that any member of the com- mittee would have the slightest personal objection to the number of members being put upon the report. Ile did not think that the adoption of such a plan would be in any wry injurious to the interests of the Society, but they must not forget that these documents vent to nearly every part of the : world. There was, however, a little secret amongst the con, mittee in reference to this matter, and it might irove more . beneficial to the interrets of the members if the cum- mittee remained the sole possessors of it. (Laughter.) A Munn.: How is it that other societies publish the number of their members? Whktilifference is there between our Society and theirs? I take the Co-opt,vaive News every week, and I find that other societies give the nmnber of their members.
A M/13111E11: I think we ought la bc told whit ig the reason tor such a course being adopted in the en of our Society, . .

... . The CHAIRMAN : The matter reefs entirely with the meet- ing. [A Voice: Oh, let's have it. (fad taught r.)] Mr. HOYLE .id that now he would tell them the secret. (Laughter and applause.) They would remember that some lew years ago the Society was at a low ebb and wanted money whereas now it was very prosperous. The cointuittee at that timi found money very .arce, and they mere almost at their wits' end for it. They knew that the Wholesale Society required them to subscribe no much per member ; and if the Runcorn Society only paid for about 806 members and happened to really have about 1,200, if they had pub- lished the number of their members they would have had to pay for the full number. So that instead of paving, say £4OO, into the IVholesale Society they would have been paying sam at a time when their treasurer was sadly in want of the other £2OO. (Applause.) The committee were quite willingte take any suggestion from the members, hut he hoped they would not meet with blame if upon the adoption of any suggestion it was found that it did Oct work well. (Hear, bear., and applause.) An amendment ins moved that the number of members should net be placed on the balance-sheet, and this was carried, the original motion being lost. A Mranne : "Where ignorance is bliss 'tit folly Lobe wise." (Laughter and cheers.) It was agreed, on the motion of Mr. Josram EVANN that the numb, of members should always be stated at the yearly and half-yearly meetings. In answer too qu.tion, the CHAIRMAN remarked that in the past the Committee hail paidtive per cent upon all loans, ' but a resolution bad been come to that in the case of any ! tom which might be taken in the future, only four per cent : should be pelt. (time, hear.) The cause of the Committee coining to this decision was that they had quite ea much money in band on loan as they needed. The Society HIM really in every flourishing condition, and they were doing la grand business. (Applause.) ! Mr. Rovrat considered that members ought to feel very !much encouraged that the Committea had been able Co declare a dividend of half...crown in the £. Certainly , they once gave 3s. mn the f, bat never more than 2s. sd. ' after that When they looked around and saw the great ' amount of competition which there VNIS in all kinds of liminess, compared with chat there was 16 or 17 years ago they mut feel somewhat astoni,thei at the wonderful anpiunt of profit made by the Society. The last half-year had been a had one astir as the general trade of the country was concerned, yet the Society had added to the rebirve fund, reduced the fined stock, and paid a good dividend. (Hear, hoar, and applause.) He hoped that every member would not only feel fully satisfied with such a gratifying result, hut proud of it. Each of them who hail got £l5 for valne in cheques would, of course, receive 15 half- crows., and those of them who had families knew what that ineant. (Applause.) He hoped they would not he NI fogish as to spend their dividend money with other tradesman, Out remain faithful to the Society ai hich had provbded such a loneflt to many of thein.

r The CHAIRYAN-believedihat the goods sold in the stores were quite as good as tit. offered anywhere else. The Committee had, st various times. heard complaints from some of the members as Co the price they. were paying for some particular article, as compared with that at which they could get it at some private tradesman's shop, hot when the matter was investigated the Committee invariably found the statement had no foundation, in fact. ; .

'Tile Bee. lietertelliiii, after stating his reason for being amongst them that evening, recommended the audience to hold high the banner af tetimerane, as without temperance neither a man or woman could he what they should be, ac- cording to the intention of their Gr.tor, who had endowed them with speotaigtita. By fait/. they were taught that!lte power of ULM had been weakened by the Sill of Adam, hut It Wee urideniable that the intud ot man was truly great. Ile cared not for tile WilVeS of the sea. or the perils of lire, if there was a life lo be saved. He tamed the roaring lion and dealt with a sure hand with the I,loa venomous snakes. lie aseamied the highest mountains-10 might have perished before hien—but the Hub made a new attempt. Fifty, sixty, ' or a hundred lives might be lost yestetday, to-morrow fifty, sixty, or one hundred new main begun , the work. The word mid the plough were in bis hands. Tile throne and the pulpit were made for man. The power of man was great, but the power of his mind was greater if he were sober and temperate. Look at the men of 40 or 60, who trembled mice those of DO. Where Wee their ' strength ? What became of the mind of the man given to drink ? It was weak and lost. altogether. Woukr they like ' to have as their physician, lawyer, or coachman, a man given to drink? The Romans did not ltdellit to their parlia- ments anyone given to drink, nor would the Snanisrds re- eeive 050 witness in Ilkeir courts of law such a person. Ily drink the power of will was lost altogether. It was there- ! fore the duty of man to stand also with Christ to destroy that sin, and he who had founded the temple a sin, indite : must try to pull it down again. 1, SERIOUS COLLISION AT ACTON BRIDGE. A GOODS TRAIN SMASHED Iro PIECES. Yesterday (Fliday) morning, about 4 o'clock, A most I serious collon occurred on the London and North-Western ,! Railway, at Dipbal Viaduct, between Preston Brook and ! Acton Bridge stations, thong!, happily unattended with any Ivan of life. From robot we were Ant to gather on the spot, the accident would seen 3 to have msulted from mreleseriess somewhere, as the facts are very simple It seems that for some reason, which we cannot discover, a , stow goods train from the Soath, due At Act. I Bridge at 4.m. was slopped at Bir.lawood, just at the end of !Dutton Viaduct. Why it was standing there is not ex- plained, as it waapow the signal., and there 'pre no signals in front of it winch could stop it there. But whilst it was ! standing an earn,se goods train from London, due about a quarter of an hoer after the slow train, came op,and passing the distant and home signals—which are mid to have hecn against Lini—dasbni into the standing Rain with great force. Whether the signals were against the express driver or not sonnet yet be proved, but the result of the collision was I me. disastrou.. Tim guard's ran of the standing train was smashed to anims,and hurled a considerahledietance,whilat • number of trucks were smashed up in a most sarprising way, and thrown over a hedge into the field adjoining the line. Fortunately for him, the guard of the standing train was not in his van at the time of the collision, or he mast bore been instantly killed. About a dozen wagon., laden with wire, were thrown into the field, and the line was covered lota considerable distance with r.e. Had the standing Gain been drairn i/p 0 few ra,ds fe.hoe south, it would have been on the viaduct which crosses the Weaver valley. and there is no doubt many of the tucks would have been thrown over the wall ~nrl would hare dropped a distanc. of 90 Ifeet. It was impossible to get at the real facia as to why the first train \CIS standing or how the second came to run in it, but it is said that the fog must Ihave been so dense that the driver of the eapress goods could not see the signals. Probably the real facts will only come out at the inquiry which will be mode. As soon as the col- ! lision was made known, break-down gangs, with cranes and I other appliinces, were sent horn Warrington and Crewe, , about 200 men b,lng at work during the early part of the morning. By daylight the up-line was cleared, and traffic Iwas conducted on the single line but the down-line was not chased until nain, the r,sult be that the newsnaper and! I many othsr trains were kept wailing until a clearance was j effecGA. The nen-sparer hair, due in Warrington at ten a.m.. did not a.sive until 13-10, ne.l ,her trains nere ! similarly delayed. The most singnlar part of the whale affair is that no one was hurt, beyond the shaking which the driver and .0000 01 the expren goods received.

div.head: MEETING OF IRONWORKERS AT WARRINGTON. ADDRESS BY MR. J. CAPPER.
div.p: MEETING OF IRONWORKERS AT WARRINGTON. ADDRESS BY MR. J. CAPPER.

On Saturday afternoon lost., large and enthusiastic meet. I beg of AVM" urkers was held in the large room Al the Uni- corn Inn, Winwick-streer, for the purl., of hearing an ad- . drehe uy Mr. Capper, and also for the purpose of considering . the advimbility of adopting some system or organisation. ! It will he remembered that in the Err:spa. r of a fortnight ,go vre announced that a dispute had taken place in the load iron trade, in connection with the fact that when an award: .4 10 per cent. advance in wages had been given bv the arbitrator for the South Staffordshire trade—Mr. ioseph , Chamberlain, M.P.— for some reason or another the advance was ref used to the Warrington furnacemeu, although War- rington has always been governed by the South Stafford- shire scale, and lathe local turns...nen could only get 7i percent. some aorenese was caused, and the men hOgran At mice to consider that they would be in e better position to obtain in the future what they term their legal rights if they were thoroughly organised. To this end Mr. J. Capper, one of the operative.' representativen on the arbitration board war invited to address the Warrington men on the working of the arbitration scheme. The large room was completely picked, and the utmost unanimity and order pre- vailed during the meeting. The CHA I µKAN having briefly explained the object of the 'Peeling, end requested 3 calm consideration of the facts Which would be placed before them, called upon Mr. Capper
nreeting.

on Mr. CorPsn, who w. heartily received, commenced hie addrees by saying he wished it to bo clearly understoml that he had not come them for the purpose of causing any dis- sension, between employers and employed, but he had at- , tended for the purpose -of explaining the working of the booth Staffordshire Board of Arbitration, and the principle , of the sliding wale of wages which had bean reeolved upon. ' After dealing with the question of capital and labour in an exhaustive manner. Mr. Capper ' went on to nay that the men of South ' glaffordeliiie with a view of settling ilisputea in a friendly and It.. confy manner, had agreed to accept the principle of arbitration in all wages question.. Mr. Chamberlain had been chosen ea Arbitrator, and when any avrard was made by ' him they had no alternative but to accept his decision. And in wages disputes which had taken place recently in Staffordshire, they were not only hound to accept Mr. Chamberlain's dezision, but it would have been most uncon- stitutional to have struck Ageing that decinion, and when- ever the men whom he (the speaker) represented acted in an unconstitutional manner, on that moment would he seek to act as one of their representatives. (Hear, hear.) More could be gained by submitting the wages question to the rinciple of arbitration than could be gained by entering into those barbarous and brutal methods which reached their climax in strikes and other meatie. (Hear, hear.) Although be was eurprised at the matinee, of the edvance given IT ' the present arbitrator ender the sliding scale, yet he bed every faith in hie honesty and strict sense of justice. (Ap- plause.) If there R. any blame attached to anyone with respect to the smallness of the last advance, that blame wag , not attachable to the arbitrator but rather to the employers. The employers at times leaned circulars announcing their ; aching prier of Iron ; and sometime afterwards when they went before the arbitrator, they would boldly and distinctly declare that their ceiling prices were wane £2 leaa than were stated or, their circulars. )°Shontr "l But the eliding scale would entirely stop such a way of doing businena as I that. which was not at all creditable to Ilion who practised I it. (Hear, hoer.) Ile had argued for some time past that I the wages question in such an important industy as the iron trade ought not to be submitted to the judgment of one into ! vidual. Ile held Hutt the principle of regulating wages by ' the sliding scale wee the best and fairest to both partici. (Hear, bear.) The principle of regulating wages in that way left the employer at liberty during times of depression or proeperity to ask or demanl that price for their iron which they thoo;lit proper, without any pressure being brought to bear upon then, by the men. By the sliding nate wages • would be regulated naturally, and much trouble and dispute would be saved. The sliding scale had been approved lay hiecolleaguee—the operative section—oil tile board of arbitra- tion. Ihe employers would prepares scale of their own, and the two would then be discumsed some time during the present month, and he should be pleased if they could secure the adoption of the one drawn up rot behalf of the nien. (Atplanne.) Less than what they asked for in that scale would not prove satisfactory to the men. They were not aching fee something with a view to a compromise or arrangement, but what they asked for in that wale they were convinced they were entitled to claim. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Capper then mail over the scale which had been drawn up for the approval or otherwise of the committee. con- nected with the Board of Arbitration, and the wale Annusl to be acceptable to the Warrington men. Mr. Capper said that the scale had only come froin the hands of the printer that day, and though he should like to are it published in the Warrie don F-rammen, bethought the publication had better be deferred until he had consulted with lois colleagues, or until it bail been laid before the employera who, as yet, were unaware of its term.. If they could get that scale adopted in ite entirety, he did not think they would have any cause to complain. (Ilear, hear.) Ile trusted that Mr. Chamberlain would give thisquestion very serious consider*. I lion, as It was a matter of great itmortance. Any scale that did not Allow ironworkers to participate in Any present I improvement in trade could not prove acceptable to the men in any part of the country. (Hear, hear., It must allow them to participate in the benefits of trade improvenients,, otherwise the men could not be expected to accept such a scale. Another quenion of importance was whet was known in the trade as the cne-fifteenth. It was a question not only considered in the Warrington district but in all districts, an'd • It was a queen. worthy of the utomort coneideration. At the conimencement of lent par an Art of Parliatnent enforced A change in the tonnage weight from 2,40(111,5. to 9,21014.., or 3 reduction of one-fifteenth. Seeing that the tonnage had been reduced one-fifteenth, the employees said they bade right to claim that one-fifteenth should be taken off the wages of the workmen. They granted them the Tight of taking it. but the mode in which some employers were deducting that one-fifteenth was most objectionable. In Staffordshire it had been arranged that that one-(fteenth should be taken from the nett tonnage rote existing at the time aloha alteration of the rater and not take it from the aggregate earning. of the men as they reached the higher atardard of wages. (Hear, hear.) One-fifteenth front 2s. ed. wan I.; from ss. it was 4d.; end front 30e. it sea. 28., that the higher they went the greater was theeacrifice. They .aid—Take the one-fifteenth frost the nett tonnage rate pre- vailing at the time of the alteration of the weight, hut do not tab, it from the aggvegate earninge of the men. (Hear, hear.) That wee what bad been done in Stefforshire. Sup- posing that a forge roller at the time of the alteration was getting Is Ad per ton, then they said—take a penny from that Is. 3.1., which will leave him Is. 21., and have all sow- ending advance* on al., t Is. 211. with no deductions what- ever. (Applause, and a ~,ice; " That's it.") That was the mode they had adopted in Fouth Staffordshire, and it had gieen very general satisfaction. Another reason why they objected to the taking of the ona-fifteenth waa because at I some places al extras were subject to a reduction of one-fifteenth. Al times men were paid extra for nmoving rolls, ten and their contention was that three extras should he ',Rid without any deduction whatever. (Hear, hear.) Ile had heard some person them ',peaking of grievance,. They would always have gri-vancea of cone kind, but they ought to have the lowan to remove acme of them. (Hear, hear.) That power' was to be found in number. end they ought to be more powerful than their employers Ile elculd not like to I see them become powerful merely for the sake of Inking advantage of their employers, but 'he nould like to see them snore "careful so that they could prevent the employers taking advantage of them. (Applann.) Ile and his friends could not onset the other representative. on the arbitration board on equal terms, owing to the fact that the masters seam members of a powerful AreWeletiOW but the reprnents- tires of the men Were not, and so they could not meet on equal terms. Ors/taint'oa on the port of the men wan a most important question. If disorganised they could not go in the presence of the arbitrot, r and give, pledge of the men)a obedience to his award, nor could the arbitrator or the employer rely upon the obedience of the men unless the 'nen were united ant bad power to compel their fellows to reaped the law. Therefore, thee ought and must become united, for cirrumnancee would force it upon them, aid the noonen they began to eet their bonne in order hie better ition would they be in when it dhl come As they ell knew there was an organisation in the north of England, hut the men of Staffordshire were going to reneganise end were going to form an independent association. and would be quite willtng to come to such an understanding with the northern association as would make thcm in their working practically one. It was propowll that the rate of con- tribution nhould he of an elastic kind. Where puddling was 7, per ton the contribution would In ad., and that slim would le the minimum ; end the contribution would inereane Id, for evely la per ton until it reached fit., which would he taken as the maximum amount of contributioe. lie then read over the rules, showing the benefits which would be derived from membership with such an organisa- tion, and said it had been arranged that in caw of a man being killed or permanently injured 30 his won, he would he allowed a sum ranging from EA to £llO, according to the length of time he had been connected with the enciety. (Hear, hear., If they took Shoffordshire, Shropshire, and Worcestershire. they would find them were at leart 10,000 ironworkers, and such a body of men combined might do each other much mottial good. lie trgefi upon the War- rington men to consider Oho matter end if they telt dimposed they could become part awl parcel of t e organisation. He was not canvaniee for •ny particular society, but be did urge upon them the necessity of selopting some n ern of sectoring their position in the future. Let them become united during the present period of proeperity, an that they would he able to protect themnelves during the next period of deprenaion. Poring the late &pension the ployers irt many Mee* were hrindicapping one set of kmen against another, hut that Wee 1 thing which should be allowed. (Hear, hear.) Men ooght always to be ri to get the full market value of their labour. He they could act upon the euggcnisns he had mad, and that they might all live to nee the dawn of better days for the ,ironer others of this country. (loud enPlem.e.) I . .

The Citataras said he wag so;; th'ey must all have been gratified with the temperate and eble address of Mr. Capper, SW he was glad to see they had a representative of the Erarniser present, as that paper, rnere than sny other in the town, reprewnnot the interrai•rd It o workingmen. (Hear, hear.) Ile was sure Mr. Capper would be glad to answer 007 question, which might be ask 1. div.head: WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS. MEETING AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS. MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

The annual meeting in connection with the Wesleyan Home Missions was held in Bold-street Chapel, Warrington, on Monday evening, when there was every good attendance. The chair was taken by Mr. John Bennett, and there were also on the platform the Revs. Charles Garrett and R. W. Starr (Liverpool), George Walker, A. Wilkinson, M. Wggal, Meuse. E. R. Bowser, W. Barlow, ho. The Come/saw, in opening the meeting, maid they all knew therm reek great call. for home miseion work through- out the land. Ile travelled through England, Scotland, and Wales, and wherever he went be found rigor of it, but wherever he went he also found that the Goepel was spread- ing. (Hear, hear.) They, however, wanted it diffused more and, no doebt, by their progress and effortx, and by their doing all they could to help on the work, they woui'd do good rervice for the Lord. (Applause.) Rev. tinonna Watnun, in reading the report, mid the home misaion fund was the oldest fund in Methodism, hay. leg been established by Mr. Weeley himself. Latit year 266 circuits were assisted from the fund, in addition to those receiving special grants. One hundred and four home mission ministers engaged in direct and specific home mis- eion work were in part sustained from that fund, of whom seven were appointed to evangelistic work—of which, he supposed, they bad one il Weld,. representative there that night, in the preeence of Mr. Garratt—(hear, hear)—and thirteen to army and navy work. The fund was provided chiefly from the yearly collection which wan made in class, by nundry congregational collections, by public meeting, and by annual subscriptions, of which they had too few in this circuit. The total income was £34,541 19s. Al., being £l,OBB 2.e. les, than the previous year. He eupposed the depression of trade had had eoniefhing to do with that. The total expenditure wait £35,586 3e. ltd., being £4045 On 3d. more than the income. The debt due to the treasurers last year WWI £7,538 Its. 3d, towards cancelling which £3,750 had been already received from the Thanksgiving Fund. By reason of the excess of this year's expenditure over the income, however, the debt had only been reduced by the sum of £2,904, and wax now £4,833 15. sd. The contribu- tions from the Warrington Circuit last year were .—Yearly collection in clew, .C 8 Sr. Ild.; congregational collections, £24 Is. RH.; public meeting collection, £4 IN. 4d.; Mr. R. Harnett', subecription, Pis.; Dr. Starkey Smith, £1 1.. the Rey. A. Wilkinson, £11..' and 15s. front Miss rendlebury's basket. There WAR belonging to last year's account the cum of £lO, which came in from the Juvenile Association too into furwthat report. The total amount reported was £5O 2s. 5d., and the £lO WhiCh CAMS in too late would make it about £BO. From that fund assistance wan given to eircuite that had to extend their operations by taking young minis- ters, and then in the course of titne provided. as they were required to do at the end of four years, an additional minis- ter'a hon.. LAW year, towards that object, of the LBO they , cent they got £4O hack; so that last year the Warrington Circuit did not to much towards the evangelisation of this country. He, however, hoped they would do better this year. (Applauee.) Rev. R. W. STARR having congratulated the chairman upon the large attendance, said it WAS refreshing to them to come from the stir and bustle of Liverpool to Warrington to solicit their ° votes and interesta " for the home Missionary Society. The Missionary Society was a capital servant of all work, and it did a vast amount of work that it never got great credit for. Ile rejoiced to know that there wee • won- derful amount of Evangelical feeling abroad, an amount of Catholic sympathy amongst clergymen of the Church of )ingland eery different to what obtained formerly. In 12 months no leas than eight clergymen of the Church of Eng- land had helped them at Brunswick Chapel, Liverpool, and he had the great privilege of attending St. Matthew's Church, next Sunday, to address the large congregation there. The good brother did not think he was going down to take his (the epeaker'e) hand, and he did not think he was going up to shake hand, with his friend. That was as If ought to be, bet it was not no everywhere. He was glad I they were looking efter their great- town, and from the reports brought home to them they found there ware Sag Amount of new life in their Methodism that did not exist come 10 or 15 years ago. The awful apathyof the multitude hail at lag broken up the awful apathy in the church. Ile took it that one of the best thirgs that came out of the home mission work was the combination on the part of God's people to do real home mission work in the neighbourhood of their chapel., end if that spirit could be developed and este, led there would be better days in the hisory of [hi. church (Hear, bear.) He described the work which was going on in the Shetland Isles, and aleo in Scotland, stating that in moat isstances the work M Scotland had been wonderfully eucceseful ; and pee a graphic account of the alleys in London. Referring to the crowded state of the houses, he mid that was in one. sequence of the removal of the houses of the poor for rail- way terminus and rnetroplitan improvements, and the people had been looking through a telescope at a foreign policy" while they had been overlooking teetering evils at home. , (Applause.) Iten. Coen. Getman maid that the recta that had been brought before them would satisfy thorn that AISTI a .citiq as their home miwionary society was *volley turdast, new had heard that night of London, but they might tmMt to the villages—(hear, hear)—and thee svouhl lind that there was great need there to presets& Methodism. Without the aid of the society the prospect of the future of Methalism in their villages was dark indeed. There were many things at work; of ovum death was busy, and it was very Radio find that the class of old Methodist farmers WAS almost dying out. He could rot help saying that they were suffering tremendously in their vill,gre from a species of persecution There wee the squire's lady. Ile did not think he was un- gallant in attacking the squire'a holy instead of the squire, for all who knew the equirearclay knew that the squire's lady was almord supreme. What was the result? There was • battle carried on by the poor people in the vihlegne of which they in nom, coulal form no notion. The other day the word went out in one nillagr that no child was to be admitted into the village day school that did not attend the ( hutch Sunday school. (Slmme.) What was to be done? He ?poke about the ladies. There were two farmers' daughtere in tbat village, and they set thetPelves to work, saying, Very well ;we will have a day school of our own.. The, went out to °Alec( money and succeeded in orcotinga place, end he had the privilege of going down to preach the open- ing sermons. He mentioned the fact to mune friends, and they authorieed them to pay off the remainder of the debt so that the school might begin without being in debt. (Ap- Ipleu..) He sympathised with the farmers who were in that position very greatly, and amked if .111 that was going on in the villages might hot they in the towns tu help them! Ought not the strong to bear the difficulties sf the week ? Ought not they to let the squires and tyrannical pareons know that sletlandiem had a hold on the people, and that to touch Methalign in the villages wee to touch it in the towns P (Applause,) Referring to London, he mid there were I40,15:1) little children who did not know where they F had to sleep that night. Ile thoLght Britannia, when she I boasted of her position, ought to hide her face with shame antil such a state of things Woe wiped away. (Applause.) In Liverpool, of 28,581 persons apprehended ho the potion last year only 352 could read and wale well:and nearly 11,000 could neither read or write at all. What one were bibles to them P He mid the brothels in Liverpool, if placed side by eide, would make • street longer than any in that town. Such things affected their Rational charecter, and they were diehonoured lofore the nations , because of those result, They affected their purees, and if they would not support the Home Missionary Society they would have to support the police. It was simply a matter of choice. They should band together to Christianise the populations of the land. What could be done? There was a great deal the State could do. The State must adopt the glorious principle of that niagniticent man Mr. Gladstone-- , (aPPlause),—and make it eary (or men to to right and diffi- cult for them to do wrong. (Hear, hear, and applause., 'they must have protection. The, must have protection againat the publican. (Hear, hear, and applape.) If the interest of the publican was opposed to the interest of the Public, then let the publican go down and•let the public live. (loud applause.) look at the Liverpool Sailors' Alome—one of the most magnific.ent building, in Great , Britain, a monument to the mundicent lilwrality of their merchant princes—erectial to protect the wailers that came into their port. After it wes erected the publi.inn surrounded it with • network of tereptetion, end within a cirele of 130 yards put di wn 47 of the moot terrible bell holes in the land. They had actually had to go out to the Borth end and buy en Wale with a prohibitory clause io thc detd against the erection of public-hou.s. It was a burning shame. Applause.) Put the publican aside and lot Jack hare a chance of saving his money. (Applause., They wanted protection apinst self-capitalists who ,t ithout regard 1011,. sufferings of their tenante would draw large rents front houaes in which people could not live. There wait an Arthane Dwelling Act, and he would not maker permiesive but imperial. (Apelause.) Thorn fewer dens should go down, and Os State should erect houses in which men could be clean, niers!, and healthy. They had far better spend their money in building houses in which there people could Ic moral and healthy, than spend- ing it in shooting Zulus and Afghan. abroad. I Applanae.) Hemmer it. for British iotoreste—(applau.)—and Britain had SORIS interest in the crowded houaes, and before con- verting the world had better begin at home. (Hear, hear.) Ile made en eloquent appeal for assistance, and concluded iniii applmse.

-- Rev. 61,01101 S WALK. said he did not think the meeting I would he fttil.fird without thanking the deputation, and he I proposed a vote of thanks CO them, as they were highly favoured in having roach a deputation. They were thoroughly experienced in the work, and he had listened to them with great interest. They could see they had come out of aver isolitical atmosphere- -(laughter)—but they were vevythank- ful to them for the very good addresses they bad delivered. (Applause.)

Mr. Atrtignws, in seconding the motion, AIM it was the electricity of the names that brought him to that meeting. He had always Itesni Mr. Oarratt nAII, extreine pleasure and had great pleasure in seconding the vote of thanks. (Applause) The motion having been heartily carrird, Ker. B. W. STAIR briefly replied. It would not only be unneceseery, but quite as Impertinent, !o Like more than a moment or two between the commencement of the meeting and the commencement of the lecture. Ile must, however, seim the opportunity of congratulating Mr. Weatherbead on what he conceived to bee very happy title. A great ninny of them were very much planned to ere that in..' of " Peace with honour," we had had pr, pounded the "Gunpowder and glory" theory as a more accurate version of the proceedingr of the Conservative Government. Though some one Lad recently owed that ,his Government had had an education in Liberalism, but whatever they called it, it was not as deep and nevem an education as what we wanted them to have. Whatever proof they wanted of the empathy he felt toward, the lecturer, and the interest he took i• his eubject, he must now amume more of the judicial attitude, for the lecture, as announced, was some- thing like plaintiff and defendant, and in Mr. Weatherhead they hail the leading council, (Cheers.) The I,9l,l7lotitsaid in standing before them ma Christian man, and desiring to speak About some of the most important topics affecting the welfare of .r nation and the world, lie wished, first of all, to define die position he assented iu re- lation to the great question Jo that announcnl for their con. sideration. 'there was a great variety of opinion aa to the advisability of ministers of religion undertaking to speak on such subjects in such a place, and some persons were very severe in their com:ernmition of those who, like himself, took interest in such affairs. Whether heron due to some defect in his mental constitution he could not tell, but it was a fact that lie had never yet learned to distinguish between the ndnister and the man. Whether a tiring WWI ministerial it aeldum occurred to him to inquire whether a thing was manly—whether it was Christion—lie did desire must heartily to know. When a nion became a Chriatian he did not cease to hen citizen, nor did he necessarily lose his in- terest in those political questions which, in God's all- embracing providence, were intended very largely to promote the good government of the world. There Wan no for. getting whose phrase •'Peace with Honour" woe. The Earl of Beaconstidd brought it back in a portmanteau when he returned from Berlin. Whatever else might be said about the Premier it could not be denied that he woe a master in the art id phrasemaking, but unhappily words with him were seldom the symbols of realities. Peacel it was a phantom. Honour ! it was a dream, and like the baseless fabric of a vision it had left not even a wrack that wmworth leaving behind. Referring to the words " Gunpowder :mei glory." he toO not know whether it had occurred to any of them to exainine that utterance of Lord Derby's with care. If language had Any meaning it implied that oneof 1110 fore- most statesmen of our time, and be a member of the aris- tocmcy And Warming to a titled clam, had been calmly considering the influence that the l'remier's rage fur Military eplendour and renown was likely to have upon the cum- , uremia' prosperity of our country, and unless he (the speaker) hod very greativ iniounderstood his meaning he in. timabd that it might net become incesairy for the sons And daughtersof 051 England, who had been barn .d reared in English homes and whose hearts' beet love had centred in the island home we all loved eo well. Referring to the But- prian atrocities, the lecturer wed on tonic that the Earl of Beaconsfield might sneer with unaffected scorer, and Parlia- ment might take its cue front those who were high in niece and loner, but the English people found their hearts stirred within them and were soon in full sympathy with right and liberty. 'The leader of that agitation woe the ex-Premier, Glailstone—(cheers, arid hear, hearl—the people's William, a man of splendid reputation And stainless clmmc- ter, and who, now that the snows of 70 winters were frosted on his brow, is full of vigour, and who, by his steillast courage and irreproachable integrity had revived in English political life the beet traditions that one age could possibly hand down to another. (Cheers.) By voice and by pen he strove to guide the thought of Englishmen into OM, common groove of syintiathy with the brave souls who were striiirgling fore larger measure of liberty l and although he wan subjec•ed to derision because of his large-heorted charity, the impartial historian would tell how lie stood up bravely for the recognition of human rights and the redress of hunian wrongs, and his name would live "1A Fanie's eternal head roll worday to be filed." ST. HELENS. --- I A very interesting entertainment was given on Monday night, in the Town Hall, IT Mr. Stephenmn's children ITOIII , the Children's Orphanage, Home and Refuge established in different parts et the country. The hall was crowded, . R1111)y hain LIM* to obtain seat aCCOmmodation. The ' entertainment e,msisted principally of singing—glee, wags, duets, memory lessons as taught on Mr. stoker eye- tem. and Mr. Stephenson throughout acted as accompanied, ! and Mr. It H. male as conductor, 3he number of children on the platform was 32, awl their excellent singing, and the ! ease and freedom with which they conducted themselve, .lled forth repeated expressions td admiration from the audience. We noticed aLso on the platform—The Revs J. A. B. Harry (Wealeyan), H. J. Weatherhead (United Methodist), and J. Brown (Preabyterian). Mr. 5nr1146!...nr, in opening the meeting, sai.l they were there to secure their very hearty eynnathy and that ratrt ‘.l • feeling which was likefy to produce some permanent help. 1 At the same time, ne wouhl let the children do most of the pleading themselves by the singing. That night's meeting would be very much of the character of a popular entermin- mem. It was sometimes his privilege in some places of worship to dwell at some length upon the religious &MI moral aspects of the work. Such remarks that night were scarcely in place. The first part of the mosramme would be sacred selection, and the rest would be more of a light character. The instil mion, which had branched out into several d.velop- ments, wag begun ten years ago by the reception of two poor hoes info cottage at London. They had now " Homes" at London, Edgeworth, Gravesend, and one for emigration purposes et Hamilton in Canada and another was to be es- tablialled near Birmingham and was intended to be ex- clusively for the orphan children of poor godly went, and was to Ge uArne.l- The Princess Alice by special desire of Her Majesty the Queen, who had always taken • great interest M the cause. These branches bad already rectiv,d about 1.00) or nearly l,f(g/ children, and about one-half of that number had already gone forth into the world to earn their own living, either at home or atroad. Al present.they hail about POO children, and He children on the platform, about 32 in number, represented those 500 for whore an appeal was made to the Chri,t inn publie. It might Ac said why come to St. Helens ? simply for this reason their work wail not local work. They had begun in London, but If was not confined to London. 01 course that vast popula- tion had contributed coneith.mble numbers of poor and destitute children to their institution . but no preference was given to children of any particular locality, for it hail al- ready received many from Liverpool, Bolton, 31anchemer, and towns in this northern hive of induatry. They had received applimations in some cases from priests of the Roman Catholic religion, and not unfrequently from Sisters of Mercy, Bible women, ladies, and city missionaries, 311n1 all sorts of people whose work br.mght them into contact with the lowest grata of the Imputation. When applications were made each case was examined by a committee of gentle- men, who after due consideration decided which waa the most needy case. They always preferred to rely upon the sympathy of the great maas ,;f Christian people. The work they carried on was definitely religious; religion was the mainspring of the movement.

of the children gave a duet. "The italin of Gilesth'' which was well liked by the audience, followed by an anthetn by the choir "Jesu, Word td God Incarnate." Mr. 5T.P11.,..N then described the mode of training. The children were not grouped altogether, which would necessitate discipline to be of the character of a drill, but they were grouped in separated bowl., by which means. as near as possible, they reproduced that true family relation- ship which wae . pleasing and natural. 'The children then sung the old song, ' Hail smiling mom," which was excellently rendered and pleased th, audience, who showed their appreciation of floe children's ability by vigor.. clapping, which was irresistible, the children being compelled to repeat part of the .ng. Mr. St.PiIYN.PN Mitt that the industrial occupation of tile children was part of their training. At the Lancsalaire branch the boys were almost all employed in farming operations on a farm of nearly 100 acres, which was pre- sented by Mr. Barlow, of Bolton. Then in the London and Gravesend branches printing was carried on, the books which the audience had then in their hands being their work. The uniforms of the boys were'aleo the work of the children. Borne more rare accomplishments were taught, such as washing their own linen, boiling potato, making puddings, which was a branch of the tine arts • good deal neglected by many of the young ladies now.a-days. The bulk of the girls would, no doubt, go out to service. SO great was the number of applic itions made for the children that he was obliged to have printed forms of refusal.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The LIALIA weekly meeting of this Board WAY hild on Wednesday, Mr. W. Winstanley presiding. The other members present were Major Cartwright, Rcv. J 1 onge, Messrs Harbyshire, Blackburst, Wallington, Cooper, Long- .), mu, woods, Houghton, Oxen, Eden, Horton, Om.nonii. John Rylands (ex-officio), and J. C. Sutton I (clerk) THY. BOARD HY NODDLE WITH WESYFCT TO ME

A Ictter war read from Mr. Mines, the schoolmaster, 'Laing that in consequence of the illness of Mrs. germotle, the indurtriAl trainer, his time had been almost wholly taken op with attending to the cooking for the children. Mr. iiLICILIMBST raid that things at the Barracks seemed to be in a complete muddle. He visited there, and never yet saw a place where things were so completely .at sloes' and sec ens." The master and mistress were busy attend- leg to the cooking instead of to the education of the children, and things altogether were in a most unsatisfact,y state. . . . . •..

The Cued abIAN complained that whenever the C'omniiitee had wanted to ilo anything they had been held up to mil- eule in the vipers and by sonw; of the members, and loaf Vole the reason come of tbein would not ant..
Several of the inembers asked who were the members of the Committee, and on this point much ignorance seemed to prevail several savingthat Mr. Wallington and Mr. Woods

Mr. LOniMHAVI said that if the children were neglected, as di were not properly fed, and their clothing and cleanli- nese properly attended to, there would be onoutbreak of fever or nom° other illness amongst them. Major CARTWRIOOO pointed out that if his advice had been taken, and 100 of the children boarded at the Kirkdale institution, at a cost of £250 week, a great sum of nmuey would have Onto saved and much unpleasantness prevents& The question of having a porter was also discussed, hot nothing definite was done beyond leavingthe matter in the hands of the Committee, whose names were read over. div.head: EXTRAORDINARY ATTEMPT TO PREVENT DISH
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY ATTEMPT TO PREVENT DISH
The formal tontines. of the Board baying been transacted without the least incident of interest, Mr. Joes Rl'utros rose and said he wished to give notice of the following resolution:— • ..

That in t. otmlon of Mk meeting Ma.. Cartwright's visit to the Runcorn Board nf Ouanilate was dlsreepeetftl te this Board, and that hie remarks about tile clerk were unjust to M. But.u. That under these elreumstancee this meeting declines re n. n the quern. of tile removal of Paulo.. Doff.. Work- house except al, the request of a ounmit tee, atd that the Chair.' man aml view-Chasm.. 'appointed a eommitt. to report on the sohjechs' •

. Mr. Rl'LltiOSsaid—Latt week when I was here a resolu- tion was unanimouslv passed, deciding that the subject in ' question should not be re-opened, without notice of motion. Major Cartwright seemed to accept that an a settlement of the question, and, act understood him to say, would not come here again; and I certainly thought that was a arise reaolution.

Major Caurrwunarr Did you? Mr. J. RPLANDS A few minutes after the resolution had been carried, I now Major Cartwright, and he told Me that he would put himself in a proper position to bring the matter forward again. and he would give notice ef motion to bring tlie matter forward again. I th -night that soon too bad, end, in order to take the wind out of his Mile, I determined I would give notice eta contrary motion. But I want to say that lam not acting merely in opposition to Major Cartwright, I can amure him that I have no unfriendly feeling towards him, but, on the contrary, I was anxious to prevent him doing whet I thought, and what other of his friends thought, was really bringing this Board into discredit. I came here solely on that ground, and finding to-day that Major Cart- wright did not carry out his intention of giving notice of the resolution he had threatened, I really felt very much in- to withdraw that resolution altogether and, if Major Cartwright will allow me, to shake hands with him, and have done with this matter. But having called attention to the fact of Mak, Cartwright's visit to the Runcorn Board of Guardians, I think this Boanl will not like to let that matter pass entirely without notice, because the impression con- veyed by the report which appeare.l in the papers is one which is clearly erroneoug, though no blame is to be attached to the newspapers, but the impiession given on reading the report seems to he that Majer Cartwright is the one member of the Board who is prepared to correct abuses, and that we, all of on are determined to oppose hint. Maio/. CIarrWMIIHT , Don't say "we." ' • "

Mr. RVIANDS It seems as lime prevented his gelling the requisite information to enable hiro to do all the goal things he wants to do. That must On the impreasion open the minds of ordinary readers.
