div.head: -CHURCHES. ANNUAL TEA PARTY
div.p: -CHURCHES. ANNUAL TEA PARTY
ST. PAUL'S _AND ST, BARNABAS'

The present season is always in Warrington essentially a I season of tea parties and each similar annual gatheringe in I connection with places of worship ; and one of the most • ' popular of such gatherings is undoubtedly the annual tea in connection with the churches of St. Paul aril St. Manahan. T it may be due to the fact that it is attended by church- . goers from every parish of the town, and by a good few Dis- senters ; but a good deal of the success is alm due to the fact that the gathering is held in the Public Hall, which thus makes it a more generally public gathering, and no doubt : secures a large attendance of total outsiders who like a good , and can enjoy a good entertainment afterwards, both of , which attraction; were provided in the Public Hall on Mon. , clay evening last, when the annual social gatherin in con- nection with the already-named churches was held. As the two churches are PO essentially one in all matters affecting their interest the congregations join in the annual festival, cod, whether dile to the augmented numbers now attending St. Barnabas or not, there was a very large increase in the number present ,It the tea. About 700 people are said to have partaken of tea, and, as [hie large number could not bosup. pliedatonce,three sittings took place, and very fortunately the committee of management had provisions sufficient to meet all demands. The tea was of an excellent character, and was presided over bv a large staff of ladies under the lead of Mrs. Wilkinson, the respected wife of the vicar. All wants having been satisfied, the tables were cleared for the entertainment, and the nuinbers present at tea were con- siderablyaugmented, about 1,000 people being present, every available seat in the large hall was occumod, and a number of people were glad to Ind standing room The after-pro- ceedings were presided over by Sir Gilbert Greenall, M.P.. and on the platform were the Rev. S. Wilkinson (vicar). Rev. E. St. A. Duke, Rev. E. C. E. and Mrs. Carleton, Rev. T. Louch, Rev. F. and Mrs. Slater, Rev. J. C. Pigott, Rev. W. H Williams, Mr. T. Sutton, and a number of others. Sir Gilbert Gretna!l opened the proceedings with a few words, in which lie espresael the ple;ssure it gave him to be present and to see such a splendid work. He congratulated Mr. Wilkinson npon the success vrhich had attended his efforts during the several years lie had been in Warrington, and said that such a large gathering could not have been brought together unless Mr. Wilkinson's heart ant soul had been with the work he had been engaged in. (Applause.) The Rev. S. WiLattosow, who was warmly received, said that in looking over the pant year he felt they had much to thank God for, especially in the fact that an few gaps had been made in their congregation during the past 12 months. They had also to thank all connected WWI the two churches for their many labours of love during the past, including the ladies who had collected the trays, the Sunday school teachers who had worked crest assiduously ; the choirs also had to be thanked for their gratuitous services, then there were the churchwardens and sidesmen, the bellringers and other officials, all of whom were deserving of their utinost thanes. He was especially pleased to be able to report that the number of scholars attending their Sunday schools were found in June last to number no less than 1132, and they had gone on increasing since that .late. (Hear, hear.) He especially mentioned the successful labours of his fellow-worker, Mr. Duke, and the organists of both churches, Mr. Pattieon and Mr. Evans. Ir. both churches there had been an increase of communicants and of con- gregation. The church of St Barnabas had been completed. and was each Sunday nseal by a large, attentive, and still increasing congregation. He referred to the fact that -I very enthusiastic lady member 01 000 of the Dissen leg churches once went into Sr. Pawl's and said, "Oh. what horrid pews ! Whytfnn'nvno hare them removed and niade as nice as we have at Wycliffe?" Well, now that St. Barnabas had been completed, he hoped they would commoner the restoration of St Paul's. (Hear, hear.) The present enormous pulpit lock-op nearly as much room as would seat twenty people, and he should like to see that re- : moveil and anew one put in its place, the pews altered. and , all seats made free, as they were at St. Barnalsas'e, where people could go, and, if they liked, could contribute towards the expenses, just as they WRIT able, but whether they did or not they were welcome to attend the church, and take whatever seat they liked. (Applause.) That was what they understood by the voluntary system. and it was what they always carried out. The alterations vrhich had been pro- posed for St. Paul's would cost about ton, and he thought that money might easily be raised. There was still much to. be done, but by their help in the future as in the past much might vet be accompliehed. (Applause.) The 'Rev. E. St. A. Drat gave a statement of the work done ; . in the !swish of St. Barnabas, where the results had been most encouraging. Ohs day schools of the parish, nose, which Mr. Finney presided, were inn most prosperous state, and the varione teachers were deeerving of every praise for , the monner M which they diecharged their duties. The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON also delivered,. brief address, anti hearty votes of thanks were ECCONIAII to the Chairman, ' the ladies, and others.

div.head: SHOCKING DEATH OF A POLICEMAN AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: SHOCKING DEATH OF A POLICEMAN AT ST. HELENS.

A very sad occitrrence, resulting in the death of P.C. John Long, °centres! on Saturday evening at the aiding of the Ravenheed colliery. Long was a supernumerary stationel at the works ; and it appears that aboest half-past nine he woe walking up the siding while sonic sluunting was going on. Seeing the engine coming along he stepped mit of the way taciding along which a number of wagone were running by means of a tail rope attached to the engine. Not observing these wagons, he was knocked down, four of the wagruns pasting over his legs, etnaehing them in various pdance, and injuring him in other parts of the body. No one now the accident, but he statist to one of the policemen who now him at the hospital, where he was taken, that he Wan standing on the line along which the wagons were tanning, not being aware that the engine and wagons were on separate lines. He lingered on until half-past twelve, when he died in the presence of P.C. DPOSOII. He bed been in the county constabulary force since 1874, and was much reepeeted. An inquest Was held on the bode, at the Cottage Hoepiml, on Monday, before tlr. Harker, depute coroner—The first witness called wee Samuel Bates, residing in the neighbour- hood of North-road, and formerly a licensed victualler. He knew the deceased, who lived at 47, New Cr ss-street. He was a police-conatable in the County Constabulary, and Won about 28 years of age.—Williem Wilton, residing at 30, Tontine-street, St. Helens, sail he was a breaksinan on the London ens! North4Vestera Railway. On Saturday night lie Woe in charge ofemue w.igons on the Ravenhead Branch, i and was assisting n shunting t' e wagona into the siding, the engine than being on one line and the wagans on another, and both connected hy a tail rope. The night was not very dark, and the nioon was just getting up. The engine stommd, and they lanced someone groan. On going in the direction whence the sound proceeded, lie found the deceased man lying on the line. He (witness) called for help, and the engine-man mme. They, however, were un- able to remove u.n. and word was sent to the copper works close by, while he went for a doctor. On the way he met Inspector Woode, who told him to secure a cab, but lie could not do so, ata; he went back without and found deceased laid upon a door ready to be taken to the hospital. The way he account rd for the accislent was that deceased was walking up the line, and scming the engine coming along, he stepped oust of the way, and, not being aware that the wagons vrere conning down a different line, and there being no lamp attached to the wag:ons, he was knocked down and run over. —Wm. Bailey, a shunter, said at half-past nine on Saturday night he wax on duty near to the place where the accident occurred, and was bolding the lever to turn the wagon, into the siding from the main line. The length of the rope by which Om wagons were drawn was about five yards. He did not remember ever seeing the slecemed. ACout half an hour before the aceidenk happened he saw two policemen ahfuut quarter of a mile away going towards Eggleston. His attention was drawn by the brmksman shouting to him. He went nor' found the deceased underneath the wagons in the four foot. but no part of the wheels were on him. He should think that four wagons had passed over him, an he was between the fourth and the fifth wagons They got some help from the Copper Works, and in about quarter of an hour they got him from underneath the wagons, and placed him upon a doer and took him to the Canal Bridge cabin. Ile bled a greet deal. WI W 39 removed to the Hospital. —Henry Eccles, the engine driver, said he dirt not know the deceased. He dill not notice any policeman standing by whilst the shunting operations were going on. When the engine stopped Rome.° was heard to groan, and the stoker said," Who's that?" Wilton went to fee, and immediately shouted,. Come he," He then got off the engine, went to the place, and found the decease,' lying on the four-foot. between the fourth and fifth wagons. Ile appeared to he enn.ions, and said, " This is an awful death to come to; I'm dying," and something about his parents, which could not be niade out. Nobody asked him while he (witness) was there ante how the accident Appened. The theory which he (witnem) bad as to the occurrence wee that the deceased bed been deceived by the engine and wagons run- ning on different lines. They worked in that manner. —Police-constable Robert Denson said that when he arrived on the spot deceased wee laid one board, and was shortly afterwards carried to the Cottage Hospital. Witness went with him and remained with him until his death, which occurred at half-past twelve o'clock on Sunday morning. Decemed was COOPCiMIN and Raid to bin, that when he saw the engine coming he stepp.l into a siding whilst the engine passed. Some wagons which were drawn by a tail-rope, and which he did not see, came on and knocked him down He did not blame anyone: Both hie lege were mutilated. —The Coroner, in summing up, said no one LAW the acci- dent occur, and therefore it Wan impossible for any witness to say how it did occur. But, fortunately, the dereased had stated to the policeman who wee with him that when he saw Ohio engine coming he slipped into the siding, and some wagons knocked him down, smashing both his legs. He thought they might take it upon the man's own word that the wagons knocked him down It being a dark night, he naturally concluded that the wagons would he on the same line as the engine. No one could possibly be to blame, as he understand that was the regular practice of working.— A verdict of 0 Accidental death" was then retumtd.

div.head: LIVERPOOL ASSIZES.
div.p: LIVERPOOL ASSIZES.

The Liverpool Winter Assizes were commenced yesterday I (Friday-) morning at St. George's Hall, before the Right Hon.J. It. C. Coleridge in the Crown Court, and the Right I Hon. Sir W. R.,,Brett in the Nisi Prim Court. The calendar I contains the names 0(R) persons. There are three charges of murder, one of manslaughter. Ms of burglary, one of administering poison, two of libel, and one of robbery, the others being of a more or less serious character.

- THE WIDNES MURDER. Mr. Justice Cotwatocx, in charging the Grand Jury, made special reference to the case against Hugh Burns (30), Patrick Keehn, (21), and Mary Ann Tracey (28), who stand charged with having, at Widnes, on the 24th October last, murdered Tracey, of Widnes, the husband of the female , prisoner. Hie Lordship arid The next me I wish to call your attention to is an extreme one, there are three persons concerned in it—two men and one woman. The woman is the wife, and they are charged with having atrociotmly murdered a highly respectable msn in his own LOUP. Ile was a workman iu very goal einpleyment, and, lov the evidence of the wiMessce in the coon,, very quiet, 'steady, inoffensive, and respeetal, man. He was • goal In.hand and father, and in every respect appears to have been an excellent man in his walk of life. There was no quarrel with the wife at all according to the evidence, and nothing like disputes of any kind. Two other persons lodged in the house, which was larger than WB5 necessary for his family and wife. The wife looked after the lodgers and the charge is that they murdered him in his bed 100 shooting hint through the head. According to the wife's account there is no doubt that he was so niurdered by some one, for he was found in his bed with the carotid artery smashed by the explosion of the pistol. His brain one roll of bits of lead—not regular bullets, but bits of lead cut off a leaden pipe; and tha pistol had been discharged so close to his head that a portion of the wadding was found in the wound. That demonstrates beyond the slightest doubt that they must have Leen in the closest possible quarters. According to the wife's account she was in bed with him, a child lying between then., when she was awoke by an explosion, and on starting up she saw nothing, but fount the room full of smoke. Her statement is that she then went to the other prisoners' room and wakened them up, and nobaly was found in the house. The back deor the raid wan found open and also the window, and according to her own statement she had carefully closed And IT,telloa both the hick door and the back window. The back window wan afterwards carefully examined by the police, and it was found to loe covered all over with a cobweb, and the sill to he thick with dust, and having no signs of having been dis- turbed, so that it lain the highest degree unprotoahle that anybody could have got in by the window. The only persons in the house besides the wife were those two men and the children. It is suggested that the wife had insured her husband's life for £lOO in seine insurance office and that he was murdered for the sake of this insurance. She stated that the person who had go:ie in had broken open the bow in which she had been keeping fifteen sovereigns, and it mutt have been sonic person who knew of the money, .d had first plundered the house and then shot her husband. Unfortunately. witness after witness swears that she wan considerably in debt to several entail tradesmen, and it is not the least likely, of course, tlmt if she had lifteensovereigns tied up in a stocking and kept in a box she would have been running £8 into debt here, £2 4s. there, when she could loavo gone to the stocking and taken out what she wanted. She was also found to have no blood upon her, :ind the child NrftB found without any Good upon its clothes. The police found the bed saturated with bloat ; and the evidence of the doctor ie conclusive on the btibjeet, for when the carotid artery is broken in that way the spurt of blood is tre- menden, and would come out over the bed. It being so an the side where the child was lying, it is almost impossible that if the deceased was shot—as he ' certainly was shot—and if the carotid artery was severed in . that way—as it certainly was—there should not hove bcen awns marks of blood ea herself and the child. There is some evidence to connect the two male prisoners with the , buying of the pistol, cartridge, and powder, but that is ' net very clear. To that, however, I would direct your par- : ticular attention. It is a most painful cane altogether ; but it may turn out, upon the investigation before the common jury— I do not say its-Ill—to be : one of those caves in which, though ones suspicious are very strong, the legal evidence of guilt may not be complete enough to justify conviction. Yourduty, however, into say if there is auch a prima facie case as, if i were substantial, would justify a fair conviction. If there is no such pima facie case, I need hardly say that by far the safer course is ' to throw the bill out, net by acquitting those people, but because it gives time for further investigation. At the same ' time, don't do that if you think there is sufficient grounds to connect them with the crime. TRIAL OF PRISONERS.

During the last epidemic they I learnt site, from its excemive fatality. that their methods of vaccination, with • view of securing increased efficiency, I might demand rigorous re-investigation. But, in spite of thme and other observations, which might he mede, tending to ! preserve a wholemtne fear in their minds and a well•con- . Metered preparedness in their conduct, be would, with equal ! confidence, affirm that, if the continom action from year to year of an energetic inspectorial department, always engaged ' in seeking out and abating nuisances, in promoting cleanli- pees about houses, in diminishing overcrowding until it nowhereexisted, and in generally supplying, especially to the poor, the neceseities of healthy living required alike by all,— he said if all this agency did not , place the country in a different torn' lon trom what it for- merly occupied, in regard to inosOns of small-pox when- ' soever they might occur, then all their elaborate and coelly sanitary Machinery was a wastef Mullion and a misleading pretence. It had been on this end other grounds,oot calling for repetition here, that the Board had suspended their Action , in regard to the means which should be provided fer the treatment of infectious diseases by isolation in a milliner so as beet to meet both the reasonably defined necemities of the ' ram and the moat thoughtful accommodation of a mattered rural dietriet. Whilst fully convinced that something tnust be done, and whilst prepared to make temporary arrange- ments of the simplest character. yet experieMe teemed hardly to have sufficiently accumithited in the country, or to ' have heen to convincing in its result, seat present known, as to juetify them in incurring a large expenditure in the accomplishment of a scheme elaborated by architects and ' doctrinaire, at a distance rather than by those on the spot practimlly acquainted, not only with the general utility of , Ruch institutions, but also with the peculiar conditione of that district. Departing from the eubject of small-pow, he hail not met with a single case of sicknem from other xymotic direame in which the necessity for hospital pre. vision had been felt, or in which beneficial resulta would ' have followed its use bad such been available. The deaths from diphtheria were four in number. They should be three only . belonging to that district, one having been imported ' from an adjoining township in the Altrincham Union. The fatal cam at Delamere would awaken memoriesof on affecting incident connected with the perilsof rural domestic architec- ture. There remained only a doubtful cam at Crowton, which led to the protection of the village well ;ands case at Moreton, where the prompt arrangemente of th, department were in- adequate to limit the extension of the disorder. Scarlet fever had been most fetal in the township of ',stock ; and Kinderton, Newton, and Whatcroft in the neighbourhood of Mitalewich. Impor.nt mnitary work, in regard to water supply and &Moors, had alwayit followed the report of these Cans. The deathe from typhoid fever in 1879 were three only in the entite diaries. which was exactly half the number recorded in 1878. Here, again, the number might be reduced one third, as one death ascribed to typhoid was of a man 84 yaore of age, who, by the natural decay of ! the part of the mystem attacked by typhoid, had long pur- chased an immunity from that complaint. The remaining two cams were of no special interest.
